'''''Yucca baccata''''' ('''datil yucca''' or '''banana yucca''', also known as '''Spanish bayonet''' and '''broadleaf yucca''')<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=134|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-06-22|title=Broadleaf Yucca {{!}} Colorado's Wildflowers|url=https://coloradowildflower.com/wildflower/broadleaf-yucca/|access-date=2021-07-07|language=en-US}}</ref> is a common species of [[yucca]] native to the [[desert]]s of the [[Southwestern United States]] and three states in [[Northern Mexico]].

The species gets its common name "banana yucca" from its [[banana]]-shaped [[fruit]]. The specific epithet ''baccata'' means 'with berries'. Banana yucca is closely related to the ''[[Yucca schidigera]]'', the Mojave yucca, with which it is interspersed where their ranges overlap; [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] between them occur.

== Description ==
''Yucca baccata'' is recognized by having [[Leaf|leaves]] {{Cvt|50-76|cm}} long<ref name=":0" /> with a blue-green color, and short or nonexistent trunks. It flowers in the spring, starting in April to July depending on locality (altitude), and the [[flower]]s range from {{Cvt|5 to 13|cm|frac=4}} long, in six segments,<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/327/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=327–328 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> white to cream-coloured with purple shades. The flower stalk is not especially tall, typically {{Cvt|1–1.5|m|ft|frac=2}}. The seeds are rough, black, wingless, {{Cvt|3–8|mm|frac=8}} long and wide, {{Cvt|1–2|mm|frac=32}} thick; they ripen in 6–8 weeks. The [[indehiscent]] fleshy fruit is {{Cvt|8–18|cm|frac=2}} long and {{Cvt|6|cm|frac=2}} across, cylindrical, and tastes similar to [[sweet potato]].<ref name="Knopf">{{cite book|last=Whitney|first=Stephen|url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/438|title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides)|date=1985|publisher=Knopf|isbn=0-394-73127-1|location=New York|page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/438 438]}}</ref>

==Subspecies==
''Yucca baccata'' has been divided into three varieties:<ref name="FEIS" />
*''Yucca baccata'' var. ''baccata''
*''Yucca baccata'' var. ''brevifolia'' <small>(Schott ex Torr.) L. Benson & Darrow</small>
*''Yucca baccata'' var. ''vespertina'' <small>(McKelvey) Hochstätter</small>

As of 2023 the status of these subspecies is uncertain. In [[Plants of the World Online]] (POWO) and [[World Flora Online]] only ''Yucca baccata'' var. ''brevifolia'' and the [[Autonym (botany)|autonym]] are listed as accepted.<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |id=270284-2 |title=''Yucca baccata'' Torr.. |access-date=16 February 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=WFO |title=''Yucca baccata'' Torr. |url=https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000752057 |website=World Flora Online |access-date=12 November 2023 |date=2023}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Banana yuccas is native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. The larger part of its range is in the US where it grows in Colorado, Utah, Nevada, California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas.<ref name="POWO" /> In Mexico it is found in three states, [[Sonora]], [[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]], and [[Coahuila]].<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=Michael |date=1 February 2026 |title=''Yucca baccata'' in Synonymic Checklist and Distribution of the World Flora. Version 26.02 |url= http://www.worldplants.de?name=Yucca-baccata |website=World Plants |language=en |access-date=16 February 2026}}</ref> The plant is known from the [[Great Basin]], the [[Mojave Desert|Mojave]], [[Sonoran Desert|Sonoran]], and [[Chihuahuan Desert]]s, plus the ''[[Arizona/New Mexico Mountains ecoregion]]'' and lower, southern parts of the [[Rocky Mountains]]. It can be found in several habitat types including [[Pinyon pine|Pinyon-Juniper]], desert grassland, [[Creosote bush scrub]], [[sagebrush]], and [[ponderosa pine]] colonies at [[elevation]]s generally between {{Convert|1,500 and 2,500|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name="FEIS">{{Cite web |title=Species: Yucca baccata |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/shrub/yucbac/all.html#DISTRIBUTION%20AND%20OCCURRENCE |access-date=2023-01-28 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref>

It is associated with ''[[Yucca schidigera]]'', ''[[Yucca brevifolia]]'', ''[[Yucca arizonica]]'', ''[[Yucca faxoniana]]'', ''[[Agave utahensis]]'', and other ''[[Agave]]'' species. It can be found among ''[[Sclerocactus]]'', ''[[Pediocactus]]'', ''[[Navajoa]]'', and ''[[Toumeya]]'' species.

The plant occurs in a large area of the North American deserts and exhibits much variation across its range. ''Yucca baccata'' specimens from the higher, mountainous regions of the [[Rocky Mountains]] is winterhardy and tolerates extreme conditions.

==Ecology==
It serves as a larval host for the [[Megathymus ursus|ursine giant skipper]], [[Megathymus yuccae|yucca giant skipper]], and various yucca moths, including ''[[Tegeticula baccatella]]''.<ref name="Xerces">The Xerces Society (2016), ''Gardening for Butterflies: How You Can Attract and Protect Beautiful, Beneficial Insects'', Timber Press.</ref> After feeding, the skippers pupate in the yucca's roots.<ref name="Xerces" />

==Uses==
The young flower stalks can be cooked and eaten, with the tough outer rind discarded. The fruit can be eaten raw or cooked,<ref name=":0" /> in the latter case resembling sweet potato.<ref name=":1" />

The [[Southern Paiute|Paiutes]] dried the fruits for use during the winter. It is still a popular food amongst Mexican Indians.<ref name="Knopf" /> The flowers are often eaten by rural residents.<ref name=":1" />

[[Ancestral Puebloans|Ancestral Puebloan]] peoples used the fibers derived from the leaves to create sandals and cordage, and the root was used as soap, although with less frequency than that of ''[[Yucca elata]].''<ref>{{Cite book|last=(Organization)|first=Archaeology Southwest|url=https://www.archaeologysouthwest.org/product/asw13-4/|title=Archaeology Southwest magazine: a quarterly publication of Archaeology Southwest.|publisher=Archaeology Southwest|year=1999|oclc=803078100}}</ref>
